settings.note: Hand-written posts for the founder's personal LinkedIn profile. English. Pillars rotate model, finance, ai, world, founder. Keep each post short; see docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-19-linkedin-personal-lane-design.md

items.hook: You are not as fast as your slowest process.
items.body:
Most companies try to improve everything. The Theory of Constraints says improve one thing: the bottleneck.

Double the capacity of every other step and the output still does not move. The press machine, the dispatch bay, the approval desk, your own calendar. Find it, protect it, then move to the next one.

Remember: a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
items.question: Where is the bottleneck in your business right now?

items.hook: Profit is an opinion. Cash is a fact.
items.body:
A company can show a healthy profit and still fail to pay salaries on Friday.

Profit sits in the ledger. Cash sits in the bank. Between them stand your debtors, your stock and your creditors.

I have watched profitable plants gasp for working capital while a modest trader with tight collections slept well.

Watch the bank balance as closely as the P&L. The P&L tells you if the business works. The cash tells you if it survives.
items.question: Which number do you check first every morning: profit or cash?

card.title: Profit vs cash
points: Debtors and stock sit in between

items.hook: AI will not replace the accountant. It will replace the accountant who never asks why.
items.body:
The machine can total, match, classify and draft faster than any of us.

What it cannot do is walk to the shop floor, notice the stock is wet, and understand why the margin moved.

The finance role is shifting from producing the number to explaining it and acting on it.

Spend less time building the report. Spend more time in the room where the report gets argued about.
items.question: What part of your month-end would you hand to a machine tomorrow?

items.hook: Some countries sit on two continents. That is not trivia. It is strategy.
items.body:
Turkey, Russia, Egypt, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan each straddle two continents.

That geography decides pipelines, shipping lanes, trade deals and who gets a seat at which table.

For a business it is the same. The companies that sit between two markets, two currencies or two supply chains hold leverage nobody else has.

Geography is not a school subject. It is a balance sheet item.
items.question: Which bridge market matters most to your industry?

items.hook: A shopkeeper in Lagos taught me more about cash than any textbook.
items.body:
He did not know the word working capital. He knew which customer paid late and which supplier would wait.

Every evening he counted three things: what he sold, what he bought, what he spent. Nothing else.

That is the whole of finance, before we dressed it in vocabulary.

Building ScoreMyBiz, I keep returning to his three questions. If a tool cannot answer them in plain words, it is not for shopkeepers.
items.question: What is the simplest money habit you have seen work?

items.hook: A small oil leak is never just an oil leak.
items.body:
The Broken Window Theory: when small problems are tolerated, they signal that bigger problems are acceptable.

Poor housekeeping becomes a safety incident. One ignored defect becomes a customer complaint. One unanswered email becomes a lost account.

Culture is not built in the annual strategy meeting. It is built by the small standards you uphold on an ordinary Tuesday.
items.question: What small problem did you watch grow into an expensive one?

card.title: Broken Window Theory
points: Small problems signal what is acceptable
Fix it while it is small

items.hook: Your money takes a round trip every month. How long is the journey?
items.body:
Cash becomes stock. Stock becomes a sale. The sale becomes a debtor. The debtor becomes cash again.

The days that journey takes is your working capital cycle. Stretch it and you need more funding. Shorten it and you free money without selling anything extra.

Collect a little faster. Hold a little less stock. Pay on the agreed day, not earlier. Three small moves, one big release of cash.
items.question: How many days does your cash take to come home?

items.hook: Treat AI like a bright new hire, not like a calculator.
items.body:
A new hire needs a brief: the context, the goal, the format, the constraints.

Give AI a one-line instruction and you get a one-line quality answer. Give it the brief you would give a sharp analyst and the output changes completely.

Then do what you do with any new hire: check the work before it leaves the building.
items.question: What is the one thing you always check before trusting an AI draft?

card.title: Brief AI like a new hire

items.hook: Being landlocked is a permanent tax on every product you make.
items.body:
A landlocked country depends on a neighbour's port, roads and customs. Every container pays twice: once to move, once to wait.

Niger, Mali, Nepal, Bolivia, Mongolia. Different continents, same problem.

Businesses have this too. If your only route to the customer runs through someone else's platform, you are landlocked.
items.question: Where is your business dependent on someone else's port?

card.title: The landlocked tax
points: Pays to move and pays to wait
Same in business: one route, one platform

items.hook: After years of signing off numbers, I became a beginner again.
items.body:
Running finance for factories, I knew what every line in the P&L meant.

Building an app, I had to learn what a shopkeeper means when she says the month was good. It is rarely about profit. It is about whether she could pay everyone and still have something left.

Expertise is comfortable. Growth usually begins where the comfort ends.
items.question: When did you last choose to be a beginner?

items.hook: Most people stop at SWOT. Strategists move on to TOWS.
items.body:
SWOT tells you where you are. TOWS tells you what to do next.

Use strengths to seize opportunities. Use opportunities to fix weaknesses. Use strengths to block threats. Shrink weaknesses that threats could exploit.

Analysis that does not end in an action list is a nicely formatted delay.
items.question: Does your strategy document end with a list or a plan?

items.hook: Revenue is vanity. Contribution is sanity.
items.body:
Every product carries a price and a variable cost. The gap between them is contribution. That gap pays your fixed costs before a rupee of profit appears.

A big-revenue product with a thin gap can be worse than a small product with a wide one.

Rank your products by contribution per unit of your bottleneck resource, not by sales volume. The list will surprise you.
items.question: Which of your products looks big but contributes little?

card.title: Contribution margin
points: Rank by contribution per bottleneck unit

items.hook: Trust AI for structure. Verify AI for numbers.
items.body:
The machine is excellent at the shape of the work: the outline, the headings, the first draft of the commentary.

It is unreliable at the one thing finance cannot forgive: a figure that looks right and is not.

So split the job. Let it build the skeleton. You own every number inside it.
items.question: Have you caught an AI number that looked perfectly plausible and was wrong?

card.title: Structure vs numbers
points: Plausible is not the same as right

items.hook: World trade squeezes through a handful of narrow waters.
items.body:
The Strait of Hormuz, the Suez Canal, the Strait of Malacca, the Panama Canal, the Bab el-Mandeb.

Block one and freight rates move before your morning tea. Factories on the other side of the world change their production plans.

Every business has chokepoints too: one supplier, one approver, one person who knows the password.
items.question: What is the chokepoint your business cannot afford to lose?

items.hook: Before any spend, I ask three questions. The third one kills most ideas.
items.body:
One: what decision changes if this works?

Two: what is the cheapest way to find out?

Three: if it fails, what did we learn that we could not have learned for free?

The first question stops vanity projects. The second stops over-building. The third keeps the failures useful.
items.question: What question saves you the most money?

items.hook: Urgent is loud. Important is quiet.
items.body:
The Eisenhower matrix sorts work into four boxes: urgent and important, important but not urgent, urgent but not important, neither.

Most careers are spent in the urgent boxes. Most value is created in the quiet one: important, not urgent. Planning, training, relationships, maintenance.

The fire you prevent never makes the news. It still saves the factory.
items.question: Which quiet, important task have you been postponing?

items.hook: Last year's budget is not a reason. It is a habit.
items.body:
Zero-based budgeting starts every line at nothing and asks it to earn its place.

Painful the first time. Then you discover the subscription nobody uses, the report nobody reads, the spare capacity everyone assumed was needed.

You do not need to do it for everything every year. Pick a few departments and start from zero. The savings fund the next idea.
items.question: Which cost in your budget exists only because it existed last year?

items.hook: A simple test for any AI tool in finance: does it shorten the month-end?
items.body:
Not demos. Not dashboards. Days.

If the close moves from ten days to six, the tool works. If the close stays the same and the team has one more screen to check, the tool is a cost.

Measure AI like you measure any investment: by the decision it speeds up or the hours it returns.
items.question: How many days is your close today, and what would it take to lose two?
items.facts: generic illustrative days, no claim about any product

card.title: The month-end test
points: Same days means it is a cost

items.hook: In India the calendar is a demand forecast.
items.body:
Navratri, Dussehra, Diwali, Pongal, Eid, Onam, Durga Puja. Each moves money, stock and credit in a predictable wave.

Shops stock up weeks before. Customers buy on credit and settle after. Transporters double their rates.

A finance team that plans around the festival calendar beats one that plans around the fiscal quarter.
items.question: Which festival moves your numbers the most?

items.hook: I build for shopkeepers in India from a desk in Lagos.
items.body:
Both cities run on small business. Both have traders who know their cash to the last note and distrust anything that calls itself finance.

Distance forces discipline. I cannot walk into a shop to explain a feature. The screen has to explain itself in plain words.

Constraints are not the enemy of good products. They are the editor.
items.question: What constraint made your work better?

items.hook: A small share of causes creates most of the result. Act like it.
items.body:
The Pareto principle: a few customers bring most of the revenue, a few defects cause most of the complaints, a few products eat most of the working capital.

The point is not the exact ratio. The point is to find your vital few and stop treating everything as equal.

Equal attention is not fairness. It is waste.
items.question: Which few items on your list deserve most of your time this week?

card.title: The Pareto principle
points: A few causes, most of the result

items.hook: Profit is one capital. A business runs on six.
items.body:
Integrated Reporting counts six: financial, intellectual, social and relationship, human, manufactured, natural.

A plant can post record profit while burning out its people, its machines and its licence to operate. The ledger will not warn you. The six capitals will.

I remember them as FISHMaN.
items.question: Which capital does your organisation quietly spend without measuring?

items.hook: If AI does the junior work, where do the seniors come from?
items.body:
Reconciliations, schedules, first drafts. Tedious, yes. Also the way every finance leader learned how the numbers connect.

Automate the task and you must redesign the training. Juniors now need to review, question and explain from day one.

The firms that solve this keep their future partners. The ones that do not will have tools and nobody who understands them.
items.question: How are you training the people who no longer do the grunt work?

items.hook: A business across three time zones never really closes.
items.body:
Lagos, Mumbai, London. By the time one office sends the question, another has gone home.

Teams that win across zones do two things. They write decisions down so the next zone can act without a call. And they protect a small overlap window for the conversations that must be live.

Asynchronous is not slower. Unclear is slower.
items.question: How does your team hand work across time zones without losing a day?

items.hook: Shopkeepers do not read financial statements. They read signals.
items.body:
Is the money coming in faster than it goes out? Who owes me? Can I pay the supplier on Friday?

That is why ScoreMyBiz turns the books into a single score and a few plain warnings instead of a balance sheet.

The accountant in me resisted. The shopkeeper in the market won.
items.question: What would a one-line health signal for your business say today?

items.hook: Your competitor is not your only competitor.
items.body:
Porter's Five Forces: rivals, new entrants, substitutes, supplier power, buyer power.

The plant that watches only its rivals gets squeezed by a supplier who raises prices or a buyer who consolidates.

Profit leaks through whichever force you are not watching.
items.question: Which of the five forces is squeezing your margin right now?

items.hook: Sales went up. Profit went down. Welcome to mix.
items.body:
When the P&L surprises you, split the change into three: price, volume, mix.

Price: did we charge more or less per unit? Volume: did we sell more or fewer units? Mix: did customers shift to products with thinner margins?

Mix is the silent one. Nobody plans for it, and it explains more bad quarters than any other line.
items.question: When did mix last surprise your numbers?

card.title: Price, volume, mix
points: Price: more or less per unit

items.hook: AI on messy data is a faster way to be wrong.
items.body:
Before any model, ask three boring questions. Is the chart of accounts consistent? Are the customer names deduplicated? Does everyone book the same cost to the same line?

Fix those and even simple tools look brilliant. Skip them and the smartest model confidently reports nonsense.

Data hygiene is the least glamorous and highest return project in finance.
items.question: What is the one data mess your team keeps working around?

card.title: Data before models
points: Same cost, same line, every time

items.hook: Two countries share a border with fourteen neighbours each.
items.body:
China and Russia. Fourteen land borders each.

Every neighbour is a trade route, a customs regime, a currency and a potential dispute. Strategy for such a country is mostly the management of edges.

Large businesses are the same. The more partners, regulators and markets you touch, the more your success depends on how you manage the edges, not the centre.
items.question: How many edges does your business manage, and who owns them?
items.facts: China and Russia each have 14 land neighbours (standard geographic count; Russia's includes Kaliningrad borders)

items.hook: The CIMA case study taught me one habit I still use every day.
items.body:
Never give a recommendation without the implication.

Not: cut the product line. Instead: cut the product line, expect a dip in revenue, free the working capital, watch the key account that buys it.

Boards do not pay for answers. They pay for the consequences you saw before they did.
items.question: What exam lesson turned out to be a career lesson for you?

items.hook: The money is gone. Stop letting it vote.
items.body:
The sunk cost fallacy: continuing a project because of what you already spent, not because of what it will return.

The machine that never ran right. The software that needs one more module. The hire you are still waiting to see.

The only question that matters is forward: from today, is this the use of the next rupee?
items.question: What are you still funding because you already funded it?

items.hook: Return on equity has three engines. Most companies only service one.
items.body:
The DuPont model breaks it down: margin, asset turnover, leverage.

Margin is how much you keep from each sale. Turnover is how hard your assets work. Leverage is how much of the business is funded by others.

Two companies with the same return can be built completely differently. One earns it. One borrows it.
items.question: Which engine drives the return in your business?

card.title: The DuPont model
points: Margin: what you keep per sale

items.hook: Before buying an AI tool, finish this sentence: the decision that changes is...
items.body:
If nobody can finish it, the tool is a toy.

Pricing decided weekly instead of yearly. Credit limits set on live payment behaviour instead of last year's audit. Stock reordered on actual sell-through.

Technology earns its place by changing a decision, its speed or its quality. Everything else is a demo.
items.question: Which decision in your company would you most like to make faster?

items.hook: In India the most important finance minister is the monsoon.
items.body:
Rain decides the harvest. The harvest decides rural income. Rural income decides what sells in countless small towns.

Tractors, two-wheelers, cement, fertiliser, gold: all wait for the rain.

A forecast that ignores weather in an agricultural economy is not a forecast. It is a wish.
items.question: Which outside factor does your plan depend on but never mention?

items.hook: Posting every day did not make me famous. It made me clear.
items.body:
Writing a short idea daily forces a choice: what is the one thing worth saying?

That discipline leaked into everything. Shorter board notes. Clearer product screens. Fewer meetings that could have been a paragraph.

Consistency is not a growth hack. It is a thinking practice that happens to be public.
items.question: What daily practice changed how you think?

items.hook: Work expands to fill the time available. So do budgets.
items.body:
Parkinson's law applies to more than deadlines. Give a department a bigger budget and the spending finds reasons. Give a project a year and it takes a year.

The fix is uncomfortable: shorter deadlines, smaller first budgets, and a review before the second tranche.

Constraint is not cruelty. It is where focus comes from.
items.question: Where would a tighter limit actually speed you up?

items.hook: The real cost of a decision is the option you gave up.
items.body:
The new machine costs more than its invoice. It costs the marketing campaign you did not run, the debt you did not repay, the hire you postponed.

Accountants book the invoice. Leaders weigh the alternative.

Every yes is a quiet no to something else. Make the no visible before you sign.
items.question: What did your last big yes quietly say no to?

card.title: Opportunity cost
points: The invoice is the smaller number

items.hook: AI does three jobs well in finance today. The rest is marketing.
items.body:
Summarise: a hundred pages of contract into the clauses that affect cash.

Classify: a month of transactions into the right lines, with exceptions flagged for a human.

Draft: the first version of commentary, the board note, the email to the auditor.

Start with those three. Measure the hours returned. Expand only when the first three are boring.
items.question: Which of the three would save your team the most hours?

items.hook: Lagos traffic taught me more about planning than any course.
items.body:
Nobody here plans a journey by distance. They plan it by the hour of the day and the buffer they can afford.

That is how good operations people think. Not the ideal time, the likely time. Not the plan, the plan plus the buffer.

Projects fail not because people were slow but because the schedule assumed an empty road.
items.question: How much buffer does your plan carry, honestly?

card.title: Plan for the likely, not the ideal
points: Buffer is part of the plan

items.hook: If you do not replace your own product, someone else will do it for you.
items.body:
Kodak built the digital camera and hid it to protect film. BlackBerry built the smartphone category and dismissed touchscreens.

Both had the advantage. Neither had the nerve.

I remind myself of this when a feature in my own app starts to feel safe. Safe is usually the moment before someone else moves.
items.question: What part of your business are you protecting that you should be replacing?

items.hook: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
items.body:
Goodhart's law. Target call-handling time and calls get cut short. Target output per shift and quality quietly drops. Target cash collection and the sales team stops selling to anyone slow.

Measures are instruments. Targets are incentives. The moment you confuse them, people optimise the number and lose the purpose.
items.question: Which target in your company is being hit while the purpose is being missed?

card.title: Goodhart's law
points: People win the number, lose the purpose

items.hook: If your dashboard is all finance, it is a rear-view mirror.
items.body:
The Balanced Scorecard adds three forward-looking views to the financial one: customers, internal processes, learning and growth.

Financial results are the outcome of last quarter's customer experience, which was the outcome of last year's processes and training.

Watch the leading indicators and the lagging ones take care of themselves.
items.question: What leading indicator tells you about next quarter's profit today?

items.hook: The reconciliation AI cannot do is the one between the numbers and reality.
items.body:
The system says stock is worth a certain amount. The warehouse floor says half of it has been sitting since last year.

The ledger says the customer owes you. The sales manager knows he is about to go bankrupt.

Matching numbers to numbers is now cheap. Matching numbers to the world is the job.
items.question: When did a walk through the plant change a number in your report?

card.title: Numbers vs reality
points: Numbers to the world: your job

items.hook: One city sits on two continents and has been a market since before the Romans.
items.body:
Istanbul. Europe on one shore, Asia on the other, the Bosphorus between.

Empires changed, currencies changed, the trade did not. Position beats fashion.

The same holds for careers. The person who sits between finance and operations, between India and Africa, between the technical and the commercial, stays valuable through every cycle.
items.question: Which two worlds do you sit between?
items.facts: Byzantium founded around 660 BC, before Rome's rise in the region

items.hook: Nobody in the market reads your P&L. Everyone reads whether you paid on time.
items.body:
Reputation in small business is a payment history. Suppliers extend credit to the shop that pays on the day. Customers return to the trader who never short-changes them.

That is the oldest credit score in the world, and it is still the one that matters most.

Everything I build tries to make that score visible to the person who earned it.
items.question: Who in your network has the kind of reputation that money cannot buy?
